quests.contextSentence: At our school, swimming lessons are compulsory for every pupil in the first two years.
quests.explanation: 'Mandatory' is a formal twin of compulsory, and 'elective' is the school word for subjects you choose.

quests.contextSentence: Five years ago she was a beginner, yet now she competes internationally.
quests.explanation: 'Pro' is the casual version of this word, while 'novice' is the formal synonym of beginner.

quests.contextSentence: We spent the whole first term on theory and never touched the lab equipment.
quests.explanation: The noun is spelled 'practice' in both varieties, but only British English spells the verb 'practise'.

quests.contextSentence: Under the new law, every employer must provide a safe workplace and proper training.
quests.explanation: The endings show the roles: -er does the action, -ee receives it. Compare trainer/trainee and interviewer/interviewee.

quests.contextSentence: Since he works full-time at the hospital, he only has evenings free for classes.
quests.explanation: Before a noun it is hyphenated (a part-time job); after a verb it acts as an adverb (she works part time).

quests.contextSentence: After five years of excellent results, the company finally decided to promote her.
quests.explanation: 'Demote' sounds harsh and is rare in speech; people usually say 'lose their position'.

quests.contextSentence: This is an urgent request, so please reply within the hour.
quests.explanation: Hospitals and inboxes use 'non-urgent' as the plain negative.

quests.contextSentence: Please don't share this link: the vacancy is open to internal candidates only.
quests.explanation: Adverts often say 'internal applicants only' or 'open to external candidates'.

quests.contextSentence: Unlike the sales staff, our support team works on-site, at the head office.
quests.explanation: 'Hybrid' means a mix of both, and 'working from home' is the casual phrase.

quests.contextSentence: Considering I paid next to nothing, I thought the jacket was a bargain.
quests.explanation: 'Overpriced' is the matching adjective: the jacket was overpriced, the deal a rip-off.

quests.contextSentence: To get the discount, you'd have to pay upfront for the whole year.
quests.explanation: Americans write 'installments' with a double l; British English uses 'instalments'.

quests.contextSentence: Unlike most chains, this company buys wholesale and then sells direct to customers online.
quests.explanation: Wholesale prices are lower per item because buyers order in large quantities.

quests.contextSentence: Since it's only a domestic flight, nobody will ask to see your passport.
quests.explanation: In business it also means inside a country's own market: domestic sales.

quests.contextSentence: The hotel says guests can check in after two, but the room may be ready earlier.
quests.explanation: As nouns they fuse into one word: check-in, checkout. Hotels and airports use both.
quests.instruction: Choose the exact opposite of "check in".

quests.contextSentence: Before prices go up, we should book the hotel for the whole week.
quests.explanation: The past tense is 'cancelled' in British English and 'canceled' in American English.

quests.contextSentence: On long trips, she treats herself and always flies first class.
quests.explanation: Business class sits in between, and Americans also call economy 'coach'.
quests.instruction: Choose the exact opposite of "first class".

quests.contextSentence: On daytime flights, I always request a window seat.
quests.explanation: In a row of three, the seat between them is the middle seat, which nobody chooses.

quests.contextSentence: You can bring one carry-on bag into the cabin without paying extra.
quests.explanation: British English often says hand luggage and hold luggage.

quests.contextSentence: On your way home, could you pick up the parcel from the post office?
quests.explanation: Pronouns go in the middle: pick it up, drop them off.
quests.instruction: Choose the exact opposite of "pick up".

quests.contextSentence: The ticket machine is out of order, so pay the driver.
quests.explanation: 'Operational' is the formal word, and 'in service' is used for transport.
quests.instruction: Choose the exact opposite of "out of order".

quests.contextSentence: By morning, the hotel had received a complaint about the noise from the floor above.
quests.explanation: Complaint has an 'a' like 'annoyed'; compliment has an 'i' like 'nice'.

quests.contextSentence: Let me talk first, and then it's your turn to ask questions.
quests.explanation: With people, talk and listen both take 'to'. 'Hear' is different, since you can hear without trying.

quests.contextSentence: Sorry, I didn't catch that — you mumble a little.
quests.explanation: No single word captures it: 'speak up' means louder, while 'speak clearly' means easier to understand.

quests.contextSentence: At this university, half of your final grade depends on a written exam.
quests.explanation: 'Verbal' can mean spoken or word-based, so it's a bit ambiguous, and 'oral' is clearer.

quests.contextSentence: It's time to get up — the bus leaves in twenty minutes.
quests.explanation: 'Lie' (lie, lay, lain) and 'lay' (to put down) confuse even native speakers.
quests.instruction: Choose the exact opposite of "get up".

quests.contextSentence: Hurry up — the film starts in five minutes!
quests.explanation: 'No rush' is the friendly, everyday way to say the same thing.
quests.instruction: Choose the exact opposite of "Hurry up".

quests.contextSentence: Every morning, warehouse staff have to clock in before their shift begins.
quests.explanation: 'Clock out' comes from old time clocks that punched a card, and many workplaces still say it.
quests.instruction: Choose the exact opposite of "clock in".

quests.contextSentence: To qualify for the exam, students must attend at least eighty percent of classes.
quests.explanation: 'Skip' is informal, 'miss' is neutral, and Americans also say 'cut class'.

quests.contextSentence: The teacher always finds a way to praise even weak work.
quests.explanation: Constructive criticism is meant to help, so the word isn't always negative.

quests.contextSentence: Your arguments are good, but this essay needs a stronger introduction.
quests.explanation: A conclusion sums things up and shouldn't add new ideas.
